                                   9                    Plaintiffs,

                                  10             v.                                          BRIEF
                                  11     ROBINHOOD MARKETS, INC., et al.,                    Re: Dkt. Nos. 103, 104
                                  12                    Defendants.
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13

                                  14          Before the court are two Joint Discovery Letter Briefs (dkts. 103 & 104.). For the reasons

                                  15   that follow, both are DENIED. As to the first Letter Brief (dkt. 103), Defendants Robinhood

                                  16   Financial LLC and Robinhood Securities, LLC (“Robinhood”) request that the court compel

                                  17   Plaintiffs Basudeb Dey and Sean Deeney (“Plaintiffs”) to produce documents and information

                                  18   pursuant to Robinhood’s Requests for Production Nos. 7, 11–17, 21, 25, and 37, and Interrogatory

                                  19   No. 13. (Id. at Ex. A.) Those requests are related to Plaintiffs’ accounts at other brokerages or

                                  20   monitoring of interest rates. Id. Robinhood also points to texts, emails, and private social media

                                  21   that might produce relevant evidence. (Id. at 4.) For their part, Plaintiffs argue that they have

                                  22   already produced information related to these accounts through their responses to interrogatories.

                                  23   (Id.) In addition, Plaintiffs argue that the dispute related to social media is not ripe, as “Robinhood

                                  24   first raised the issue of Dey’s purportedly relevant Facebook posts on February 9, two days before

                                  25   the parties’ February 11 conferral” and where “[t]o date, Robinhood has never proposed any

                                  26   search terms” and failed to engage. Id.

                                  27          Rule 26(b)(1) governs the scope of discovery in federal cases and provides that parties may

                                  28   obtain discovery regarding any nonprivileged matter that is relevant to any party’s claim or
                                         Case 3:24-cv-07442-RFL           Document 108         Filed 03/06/26      Page 2 of 3




                                   1   defense. Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(1). With respect to the first Letter Brief (dkt. 103), as Plaintiffs

                                   2   point out, the case “will be resolved by an objective determination of whether Robinhood

                                   3   breached the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, or was otherwise unfair.” Id. at 4.

                                   4   The court agrees. Considering the claims in this case, the impending discovery deadline of March

                                   5   31, 2026, for substantial completion of discovery (dkt. 101 at 2), the financial information already

                                   6   provided through interrogatory responses, and the burden and invasiveness associated with

                                   7   producing texts, emails, and the requested personal financial account documents, the court finds

                                   8   the request overbroad and unduly burdensome. Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(1). This is especially true

                                   9   where several social media posts are already public, and the value of any of the private

                                  10   information is low in comparison to the needs of the case. Accordingly, Robinhood’s Letter Brief

                                  11   (dkt. 103) is DENIED.

                                  12          As to the second Letter Brief (dkt. 104), Plaintiffs are seeking documents and information
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   related to Robinhood’s U.K. Program, such as documents related to how Robinhood set fees and

                                  14   interest rates in its Robinhood U.K. Brokerage Cash Sweep Program. (Id. at 4.) However,

                                  15   Robinhood asserts that this is a class action regarding Robinhood’s “U.S.-based deposit sweep

                                  16   program (the “Program”) proposing to represent a U.S.-based class.” (Id. at 6.) Robinhood further

                                  17   points out that it has “already produced internal documents comparing the Program to other U.S.-

                                  18   based cash sweep programs and alleged benchmarks like the federal funds rate, as well as internal

                                  19   documents reflecting Robinhood’s decision-making process with respect to the U.S.-based

                                  20   Program” and that “[i]f there are documents in the review population comparing the U.S. Program

                                  21   to the U.K. program, those documents will also be produced.” (Id. at 7.) Robinhood also provides

                                  22   that it has already produced “approximately 10,000 documents to date and anticipates producing

                                  23   tens of thousands more before the March 31 substantial completion deadline.” (Id. at 6.) The court

                                  24   finds that the U.K. Program, which operates in a different country with a different legal regime

                                  25   and market, is at best tangentially relevant to the claims here. Rule 26(b)(1) requires the court to

                                  26   enter a balancing test including, among other factors, the parties’ resources and access to the

                                  27   information, the importance of the discovery at issue, and the “whether the burden or expense of

                                  28   the proposed discovery outweighs its likely benefit.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(1). Considering the
                                                                                          2
                                         Case 3:24-cv-07442-RFL           Document 108         Filed 03/06/26      Page 3 of 3




                                   1   factors in this rule, as well as the short discovery timeline in this case noted above, the court finds

                                   2   that the request here—which Plaintiffs admit could only be captured in if the scope of discovery is

                                   3   “broad”—is overbroad and burdensome. Accordingly, Plaintiffs’ Letter Brief (dkt. 104) is

                                   4   DENIED.

                                   5

                                   6   IT IS SO ORDERED.
